lessonRef.subject: mathematics
lessonRef.unitTitle: Systems of Linear Equations and Inequalities
lessonRef.focus: graphing half-planes as inequality solution sets
lessonRef.title: Discussion or problem seminar: graphing half-planes as inequality solution sets

sections.title: Instructional examples
sections.directions: One approach is shown. There is at least one other that works.

items.prompt: Why may we add a multiple of one equation to another?

steps: Every common solution still satisfies the combination.
The step reverses, so nothing is gained.

sections.title: Guided practice
sections.directions: For each, name a second method before you solve it.

items.prompt:
How many solutions does this system have?
  2x − 2y = 11
  6x − 6y = 38

sections.title: Independent practice
sections.directions: Work on your own. Show the steps that produced each answer.

items.prompt: Is the point (-4, -5) in the solution region of -7x − 2y ≤ 2?
choices: The region cannot be tested without graphing it first.
No; substituting gives 38, which is greater than 2.
Only points on the boundary line are in the solution region.

items.prompt: A student replaces the second equation of a system with (second equation) + 5 × (first equation). Which statement is correct?
choices: The new system has exactly the same solution set, because the replacement step is reversible.
The new system may lose solutions that the original had.
The new system is equivalent only when 5 is 1.
The new system may gain solutions that the original did not have.

sections.title: Extension and challenge
sections.directions: Argue for one method over another. Say what makes it better, not just that it is.

items.responseExpectation: Give the result and the reasoning that produced it. Show enough work that someone else could check each step.

items.prompt:
How many solutions does this system have?
  3x − 2y = -11
  4x − 2y = -8
items.responseExpectation: Give the result and the reasoning that produced it. Show enough work that someone else could check each step.
